APL synapses project · step-by-step reports · Report 12 · 2026-10-24

APL confined to its calyx sub-arbors

QuestionIf signals inside APL cannot cross between its calyx sub-arbors (the compartments of Report 10), does the model reshape the KC representation, especially the rank order of odor-pair similarity with inhibition on versus off, more like TNT vs TNT3c than a uniform APL, an APL weighted by per-KC synapse counts, or the local APL without walls of Report 11?

  • APL skeletons and calyx sub-arbors (Report 10)
  • Calyx KC ↔ APL and APL → PN synapses with their positions (Reports 01, 02)
  • The local model of Report 11, as reference

Report 10 found that APL's calyx arbor is not one continuous tree in the calyx: it comes in several sub-arbors that join only farther down, through the peduncle or the lobes, so two synapses in different sub-arbors are 200–360 µm apart along APL even when they are close in space. Report 11 let APL's signal fade smoothly with distance along the skeleton. This report tries the other extreme suggested by that anatomy: each sub-arbor is a closed compartment, and a KC's activity can only inhibit KCs whose APL synapses sit in the same sub-arbor. Hemibrain R, male CNS L and R (Yang, 2026-10-21), both versions of the tables.

1The compartments: APL's calyx sub-arbors

The compartments are exactly the sub-arbors of Report 10. Skeleton nodes within 5 µm of a calyx APL synapse (from the table with synapses outside the official ROIs added, which covers the whole calyx) are calyx nodes. Keeping only those nodes and the skeleton edges between two of them splits APL's calyx arbor into connected pieces, because the pieces are joined only through nodes outside the calyx. Each piece is one compartment. Pieces holding at least 2% of APL's synapses on microglomeruli keep Report 10's names S1, S2, …; the rest are small pieces, and each small piece is a compartment of its own. Every calyx KC ↔ APL synapse is placed at its nearest skeleton node and so belongs to exactly one compartment (none fell outside a piece).

Table 2. Compartments, official ROIs. Effective number = 1/∑csc21/\sum_c s_c^21/∑c​sc2​ with scs_csc​ the compartment's share of APL → KC synapses (equal to the count if all were equal). The last two columns use each KC's synapses with APL in both directions.
Mushroom bodycompartments with KC synapsesnamed (≥ 2%)effective numberlargest share of APL → KCKC main-compartment share, medianKCs entirely in one compartment
hemibrain R1651.873%0.7212%
male CNS L1565.330%0.6411%

Hemibrain R has one dominant compartment (effective number 1.8), so walls change little there; male CNS L is split most evenly. Most KCs have their APL synapses in more than one compartment, because a KC's claws are spread over the calyx, but usually with a clear main one (median share 0.72 in hemibrain R, 0.64 in male CNS L, 0.73 in male CNS R).

2The model, step by step

2.1Step 1: KC input and pinning (unchanged)

As in Reports 07 and 11: each KC's input is its claws' PN synapse shares times the glomerular ORN (or GH146) responses; each odor's input gain is set so that with APL blocked the fraction of KCs responding equals that odor's TNT fraction; the blocked responses ykoblocked=[xko−1]+y^{\mathrm{blocked}}_{ko} = [x_{ko} - 1]_+ykoblocked​=[xko​−1]+​ are the same for every version.

2.2Step 2: feedback through a coupling matrix

yko  =  [ xko−θ−a∑jMkj yjo]+(1)y_{ko} \;=\; \Big[\, x_{ko} - \theta - a \sum_{j} M_{kj}\, y_{jo} \Big]_+ \tag{1}yko​=[xko​−θ−aj∑​Mkj​yjo​]+​(1)
The steady state of KC responses with APL intact, solved per odor. Versions differ only in MMM.

Isopotential compartments (λ=∞\lambda = \inftyλ=∞). Inside one compartment the APL potential is the same everywhere; nothing passes between compartments. KC jjj raises the potential of compartment ccc in proportion to its KC → APL synapses there, IcjI_{cj}Icj​, and KC kkk is inhibited by that potential at its APL → KC synapses there, OckO_{ck}Ock​:

Mkj  =  const×∑cOck Icj(2)M_{kj} \;=\; \mathrm{const} \times \sum_{c} O_{ck}\, I_{cj} \tag{2}Mkj​=const×c∑​Ock​Icj​(2)
A sum over compartments of per-compartment "C" matrices. With a single compartment this is exactly C.

Isopotential, divided by cable length ("÷ length"). A passive compartment of membrane area AAA turns an input current into a voltage change in proportion to its input resistance, which scales as 1/A1/A1/A. Taking area proportional to cable length LcL_cLc​ (same branch thickness), the same input moves a small compartment's potential more than a large one's:

Mkj  =  const×∑cOck IcjLc(3)M_{kj} \;=\; \mathrm{const} \times \sum_{c} \frac{O_{ck}\, I_{cj}}{L_c} \tag{3}Mkj​=const×c∑​Lc​Ock​Icj​​(3)
LcL_cLc​ in µm; a piece with no edge counts as 1 µm.

Decay inside compartments (λ\lambdaλ = 200, 100, 50, 25, 10 µm). The local model of Report 11, with every skeleton edge that leaves a compartment cut:

Mkj  =  const×∑s ∈ out(k)  ∑t ∈ in(j)1[ c(s)=c(t) ]  e−d(s,t)/λ(4)M_{kj} \;=\; \mathrm{const} \times \sum_{s \,\in\, \mathrm{out}(k)} \; \sum_{t \,\in\, \mathrm{in}(j)} \mathbf{1}[\,c(s) = c(t)\,]\; e^{-d(s,t)/\lambda} \tag{4}Mkj​=const×s∈out(k)∑​t∈in(j)∑​1[c(s)=c(t)]e−d(s,t)/λ(4)
out(k)\mathrm{out}(k)out(k): APL → KC sites on KC kkk; in(j)\mathrm{in}(j)in(j): KC → APL sites of KC jjj; c(s)c(s)c(s): compartment of site sss.

In each version the constant sets the mean of MMM to that of C; the gain calibration (Step 4) would absorb it anyway.

2.3Step 3: computing M on the tree with walls

The two-pass computation of Report 11 (pass 1 from the leaves up, pass 2 from the root down, each edge vvv weighted by κv\kappa_vκv​) gives Φvj=∑te−d(v,t)/λ\Phi_{vj} = \sum_t e^{-d(v,t)/\lambda}Φvj​=∑t​e−d(v,t)/λ exactly on a tree. Walls are added by setting κv=0\kappa_v = 0κv​=0 on every edge whose two ends are not in the same compartment; a signal can then never cross that edge. Because the path between two nodes of one connected piece stays inside the piece, an edge of the reduced tree that joins two nodes of the same compartment never leaves it, so this test on the reduced tree is exact. For λ=∞\lambda = \inftyλ=∞ (κv\kappa_vκv​ = 1 inside), the result was compared with ∑cOc⊤Ic\sum_c O_c^{\top} I_c∑c​Oc⊤​Ic​ computed directly: identical in all three mushroom bodies (difference exactly 0).

2.4Step 4: gains, solver, bouton route

For every mushroom body, input table and version, the gain aaa is found by bisection so that the mean fraction of KCs responding equals TNT3c's (6.83% for the 16 odors), with the exact active-set solver of Report 11. The bouton route of Report 11 is kept, with the APL signal at each bouton taken from the same walled computation (QboQ_{bo}Qbo​ from Φ\PhiΦ at its APL → PN synapses): boutons only (all inhibition on boutons) and KCs + boutons at the boutons' real share fff of APL's calyx output, for λ\lambdaλ = ∞ and 50 µm.

2.5Step 5: readouts and null

  • Rank order ρrank\rho_{\mathrm{rank}}ρrank​, pattern rrr and size (mean ΔS), exactly as in Report 11. Data: ρrank\rho_{\mathrm{rank}}ρrank​ = 0.869 (ORN odors) and 0.873 (GH146 odors), about 0.92 after correcting for recording noise; rrr can reach about 0.84 at most; mean ΔS 0.178 and 0.201.
  • Null: for the isopotential version (∞ or ∞ ÷ length) with the better rrr, KCs swap their APL synapse sites with other KCs of the same class (KC kkk gets KC π(k)\pi(k)π(k)'s sites, M→Mπ(k)π(j)M \to M_{\pi(k)\pi(j)}M→Mπ(k)π(j)​), 100 times, recalibrating each time. This asks whether it matters which KC sits in which compartment. One-sided ppp = (1 + shuffles at least as extreme) / 101.

3What walls do to the coupling

With isopotential compartments 6% of KC pairs in hemibrain R, 46% of KC pairs in male CNS L, 26% of KC pairs in male CNS R cannot interact at all, yet a typical KC is still inhibited by 66%, 30%, 50% of all KCs (same order), because its synapses lie in the big compartments. At λ = 10 µm the walled and unwalled matrices are practically the same (the signal has faded long before it would reach another compartment, 200–360 µm away), so from about 25 µm down this model and Report 11's coincide.

Answer, official ROIs

Rank order: no. Confined to sub-arbors, inhibition on KCs leaves ρrank\rho_{\mathrm{rank}}ρrank​ at 0.979–0.987 (ORN) and 0.976–0.983 (GH146), next to U (0.977, 0.983) and C (0.984, 0.984), and far above the data's ≈ 0.92. Inhibition on boutons only, confined to sub-arbors, reaches 0.966 (ORN), 0.937 (GH146) at λ = ∞, against 0.957, 0.931 without walls (Report 11): the walls do not make it reorder more. With KCs and boutons at the real share it is back to 0.985, 0.980.

Pattern: better than one APL only when small compartments count more, and never better than without walls. Isopotential compartments give rrr = 0.469 (ORN), 0.230 (GH146), no better than C; dividing each compartment's potential by its cable length gives 0.503, 0.399, against U 0.455 / 0.316, C 0.475 / 0.319 and the best local version without walls 0.581 (λ = 5 µm, ORN), 0.528 (λ = 2 µm, GH146). With decay inside compartments rrr rises as λ shrinks, but only to the values the same λ gives without walls.

Placement within compartments: shuffling KCs within class for ORN (λ = ∞, ÷ length), GH146 (λ = ∞, ÷ length) gives ORN: rrr 0.503 vs shuffles 0.420, ppp = 0.13; GH146: rrr 0.399 vs shuffles 0.233, ppp = 0.01.

Size: no. Mean ΔS of the KC-route compartment versions is 24%–26% of the data's (ORN), 14%–17% of the data's (GH146), smaller than U's.

The walls matter only where the signal would otherwise reach another sub-arbor, at long λ (∞ to 50 µm). There they change ρrank\rho_{\mathrm{rank}}ρrank​ by −0.002 to +0.003 and rrr by −0.089 to +0.006 (mostly lowering it, most for GH146). At λ = 10 µm walled and unwalled rrr agree to three decimals.

With KCs and boutons at the real share it is back to 0.978, 0.979.

Isopotential compartments give rrr = 0.500 (ORN), 0.322 (GH146), no better than C; dividing each compartment's potential by its cable length gives 0.558, 0.490, against U 0.500 / 0.342, C 0.512 / 0.388 and the best local version without walls 0.596 (λ = 2 µm, ORN), 0.545 (λ = 2 µm, GH146). 6What this means, and caveats

  • Confining APL's signal to its calyx sub-arbors does not make inhibition reorder odor pairs more. The rank order stays at about 0.98, like a uniform APL. In this model, inhibition that acts on the KCs, whether global, local or split into compartments, mostly rescales KC responses and keeps the order of similarities (Report 09 explains when that happens).
  • For which pairs change most, walls alone do not help: isopotential compartments match the data no better than one APL. Only when each compartment's potential is divided by its cable length, so that small compartments respond more strongly, does rrr rise above U and C, and for GH146 input that version beats within-class shuffles in both versions of the tables (for ORN it does not). It still stays below Report 11's local model without walls at short λ, and at short λ the walls are irrelevant because the signal fades before reaching another sub-arbor.
  • The sub-arbors are uneven: hemibrain R is nearly one compartment, so most of any effect would come from male CNS. Most KCs have synapses in more than one compartment, which spreads each KC's inhibition over several compartments and blurs the walls.
Caveats

The sub-arbors come from the skeletons' connectivity. A connection missed by the segmentation, or a false merge, would change them (Report 10); worth checking in neuroglancer before relying on them.

Every small piece is treated as its own compartment. They hold 1–4% of APL's synapses, so pooling them differently would change little.

"÷ length" assumes the same branch thickness everywhere; real input resistance also depends on thickness and on the connections through the peduncle, which the walls ignore.

Synapse counts stand in for strength; a steady state is assumed; the shuffle ppp values do not correct for choosing between the two isopotential versions.
